questions.prompt: When \(A\) has full column rank, the least-squares solution of \(Ax \approx b\) is the solution of
questions.explanation: The gradient of \(\lVert Ax - b\rVert^2\) is \(2 A^T(Ax - b)\). Setting it to zero is the normal equation \(A^T A x = A^T b\). Full column rank makes \(A^T A\) invertible, so there is one solution. The system \(Ax = b\) is overdetermined and need not be consistent. \(AA^T\) is the Gram matrix of the rows, the wrong shape for a tall full-column-rank \(A\). The residual is zero only when \(b\) is in the column space.

questions.figure_alt: A small array with two short rows of labels.
options: \(Ax = b\), which is always a consistent square system

questions.prompt: Four measurements of one unknown are \(2, 4, 6, 8\). The model is that unknown times a column of ones. What is the least-squares value?
questions.explanation: The normal equation is \(4 x = 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20\), so \(x = 5\). That is the average. Reporting \(20\) gives the sum. Reporting \(8\) or \(2\) gives an endpoint. The residual is not zero: the four numbers are not equal. The column of ones has full column rank, so the average is the unique minimizer of the sum of squares.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: \(A^T A\) is positive definite exactly when
questions.explanation: \(x^T A^T A x = \lVert Ax\rVert^2\) is positive for every \(x \ne 0\) exactly when \(Ax = 0\) has only the zero solution, which is full column rank. Extra rows do not prevent two columns from being copies of each other. A square matrix can be singular. The right-hand side \(b\) does not enter \(A^T A\).

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that derives the normal equations for \(\lVert Ax - b\rVert^2\). Each step uses the previous result.
questions.explanation: The objective is expanded before it is differentiated. The gradient is the quantity set to zero. Canceling \(2\) is legal only after that equation exists, and the rearrangement is the normal equation. Setting \(Ax - b = 0\) instead of the gradient to zero demands an exact fit the data may not have. Differentiating before writing the objective has nothing to differentiate.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: Write the objective as \((Ax - b)^T(Ax - b)\).
Differentiate it in \(x\). The gradient is \(2 A^T(Ax - b)\).
Set that gradient equal to zero.
Cancel the nonzero factor \(2\) and rearrange to \(A^T A x = A^T b\).

questions.prompt: Let \(A\) have rows \((1, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), \((0, 1)\), \((0, 1)\) and let \(b = (3, 5, 2, 6)\). The least-squares solution is \((4, 4)\). Which claims hold?
questions.explanation:
\(A^T A = 2I\), and \(A^T b = (8, 8)\), so the normal equation gives \((4, 4)\).
• The residual \((-1, 1, -2, 2)\) dots to zero with each column, which is \(A^T(Ax - b) = 0\).
• \(A^T A\) is invertible, so the columns are independent and the Hessian \(A^T A\) is not singular.
• \(Ax = (4, 4, 4, 4)\) is not \(b\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a two-column array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">b   n</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   0</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A small array with two short rows of labels.
options: \(A^T A x = A^T b\) holds at \((4, 4)\).
The residual is orthogonal to both columns of \(A\).
The Hessian of \(\tfrac12\lVert Ax - b\rVert^2\) is singular.

questions.prompt: A single column \((p, q)\) and a right-hand side \((u, v)\) give a scalar unknown. The normal-equation solution equals
questions.explanation: The normal equation is \((p^2 + q^2) x = p u + q v\). The column is nonzero on the declared ranges, so the division is legal and every name is used. This is the same number as the orthogonal projection of \((u, v)\) onto the span of \((p, q)\), divided out to a coefficient. Swapping the denominator for \(p + q\) is not the Gram entry. Dropping a product in the numerator drops one row of \(A^T b\).

questions.prompt: A note derives the normal equations. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The gradient formula is right, and clearing it really does produce \(A^T A x = A^T b\). Full column rank really does invert \(A^T A\). The false step replaces \(A^T b\) by \(b\). Those two vectors have different shapes whenever \(A\) is not square, and they are different even when a square \(A\) is invertible. The right-hand side has to be \(A^T b\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: The gradient of \(\lVert Ax - b\rVert^2\) is \(2 A^T(Ax - b)\).
Setting that gradient to zero is equivalent to \(A^T A x = A^T b\).
The same equation can be written \(A^T A x = b\).
Full column rank makes \(A^T A\) invertible.
reasons: The right-hand side is \(A^T b\), not \(b\).
The gradient is \(2A(Ax - b)\), without a transpose.
Full column rank leaves \(A^T A\) singular.

questions.prompt: Let \(A\) have rows \((1, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), \((0, 1)\), \((0, 1)\), and let \(b = (3, 5, 2, 6)\). The least-squares solution is \((4, 4)\). What is the squared residual \(\lVert Ax - b\rVert^2\)?
questions.explanation: The fitted vector is \((4, 4, 4, 4)\). The residual is \((-1, 1, -2, 2)\), and the sum of squares is \(1 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 10\). Reporting \(4\) gives a coordinate of the solution. Reporting \(8\) is \(A^T b\)'s common entry. Reporting \(0\) would be an exact fit, and these four numbers are not constant on each column. The normal equation already fixed the solution. This number is only the objective at that solution.

questions.prompt: When \(A\) has full column rank, the least-squares solution is
questions.explanation: Full column rank inverts the smaller Gram matrix \(A^T A\), and the solution is \((A^T A)^{-1} A^T b\). The formula with \((AA^T)^{-1}\) belongs to a full-row-rank matrix, which is short and wide. A nonsquare \(A\) has no inverse. \((AA^T)^{-1} b\) is not even the right shape to be an \(x\) in the column space of a tall \(A\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a two-column array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">b   n</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   0</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A small array with two short rows of labels.
options: \(A^T (A A^T)^{-1} b\), the formula for a full-row-rank matrix
\(A^{-1} b\), whether or not \(A\) is square

questions.prompt: Which model, with parameters collected in one vector, is linear in those parameters?
questions.explanation: A line is a dot product of \((m, c)\) with \((t, 1)\). The design matrix does not depend on the parameters. An exponential, a sine, or a power hides the parameter inside a nonlinear function. Those fits are nonlinear least squares. The line, once there are more points than coefficients, is an ordinary normal equation.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Fit \(y = a + b t\) to the three points \((t, y) = (1, 2),\ (2, 3),\ (3, 6)\) by least squares. What is the slope \(b\)?
questions.explanation: The normal matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}\) and the right-hand side is \((11, 26)\). The second unknown comes out to \(2\), and the intercept is \(-1/3\). Check: \(3a + 6b = 11\) becomes \(3a + 12 = 11\) when \(b = 2\), so \(a = -1/3\), and \(6a + 14b = -2 + 28 = 26\). Reporting \(-1/3\) gives the intercept. Reporting \(6\) or \(3\) gives a data coordinate. The fit is not exact, but the slope of the least-squares line is \(2\).

questions.prompt: If the columns of \(A\) are linearly dependent, the normal equations
questions.explanation: \(A^T b\) is always in the column space of \(A^T A\), so the normal equations stay consistent. Dependence makes \(A^T A\) singular, and the solution set is a translate of the null space: infinitely many solutions, all with the same residual. The residual is zero only when \(b\) is in the column space of \(A\). Dependence does not force that.
